title: Every Humanoid Robot Needs Rare-Earth Magnets. Here's the American Stock Positioned to Sell Them -- and It's Down 62%.
detail:
Every Humanoid Robot Needs Rare-Earth Magnets. Here's the American Stock Positioned to Sell Them -- and It's Down 62%.
Keith Noonan, The Motley Fool

TSLA
NVDA
688836.SS
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The rise of humanoid robots could be one of the next decade's most important technology trends. Tesla is betting heavily on its Optimus robots and expects humanoid robotics to become its most important product category. Meanwhile, Chinese pure plays including Unitree Robotics are also aiming to build leading positions in the fledgling tech category.

Rising demand for humanoid robots is set to push demand for rare-earth minerals and magnets even higher because these elements and composites are crucial foundations for some of the capabilities that make these robots special. There's a catch, though. Geopolitical dynamics and broader supply constraints mean that sourcing rare-earth materials and magnets could be very difficult -- especially for U.S.-based companies.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The good news is that MP Materials (NYSE: MP) is positioning itself to address this potentially huge supply chain issue, and it could wind up delivering big wins for patient investors.

Image source: Getty Images.
Rare-earth materials have become a crucial supply chain variable

While the U.S. and China maintain formal diplomatic relations, it's no secret that the two countries are the foremost competing world powers and are taking steps to gain an edge over each other. Along those lines, China's control over the extraction, refinement, and production of usable rare-earth minerals and magnets is a strength that the country is leveraging against the U.S. and its allies.

According to some estimates, China is responsible for roughly 60% of global rare-earth mining and 90% of processing. China is already using its stranglehold on the rare-earth market as a trade and geopolitical bargaining chip, and it could completely block exports if relations with the U.S. worsen. That could deal a crushing blow to U.S.-based manufacturers of humanoid robots.

According to MP Materials CEO James Litinsky, each humanoid robot will need between 8 and 10 pounds of rare-earth-magnet content in order to facilitate movement across various articulated joints. On a comparative basis, this works out to between double and triple the amount found in electric vehicles.

Litinsky believes that humanoid robots will become a major economic and defense sector resource for the U.S., and that means that his company could be poised to enjoy surging demand and pricing power. Meanwhile, the company's share price is down roughly 62% from its high amid concerns about whether the company's growth bets will come to fruition and doubts about just how much pricing power MP will actually be able to command in the rare-earth magnets space.

title: Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue

Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue

Every member of Wall Street's "Magnificent Seven" now wants its stock kept off OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue.

Apple and Meta Platforms are among 11 companies added to the list of objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Thursday.

They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla, completing a sweep by the group of tech giants that makes up a large share of the S&P 500's value. The other new objectors are Home Depot, Boeing, GE Vernova, Palantir, ServiceNow, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Nebius Group, bringing the total number of companies saying "no" to the OKX and ICE platform to 67.

Meta's objection carries some irony. The Facebook parent once tried to launch its own stablecoin, Libra, later renamed Diem, before abandoning the project in 2022 amid regulatory pushback.

Apple had been one of the last megacaps missing from the list after Amazon, Tesla, and SpaceX objected in the venue's Nov. 2 notice. The tally stood at 56 then, and at nine on Oct. 15, when the first objectors appeared.

Just as notable is who hasn't objected. Crypto-friendly public companies such as Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy don't appear on the list. Coinbase launched tokenized stocks for non-U.S. users on its Base network in August. Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, and Exxon Mobil are also absent. It's unclear whether OKXICE notified those companies.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. It's worth noting, though, that the objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. An outside "tokenizer" would hold real shares one-for-one through a registered broker-dealer.

With the market's biggest names opted out, it's unclear which major stocks the venue will be able to offer at launch, and its notices don't list the tokens it plans to make available.

title: Prediction: Here's What a $1,000 Investment in Rivian Will Be Worth by 2030 if the R2 Ramp Holds

Prediction: Here's What a $1,000 Investment in Rivian Will Be Worth by 2030 if the R2 Ramp Holds
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool

NVDA

Rivian (NASDAQ: RIVN) hasn't exactly been hiding the fact that it is using Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) playbook. And the R2 is a significant step along the path Tesla blazed. Which is why it is such good news that the R2 is now Rivian's best-selling vehicle. If Tesla is the example, investors could see Rivian's stock price rocket by as much as 1,000% if the good news keeps rolling in.

But through 2030, more modest expectations are probably appropriate. Here's why I think Rivian's stock could double or even triple over the next three years or so.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
What's going on with Rivian?

Like Tesla, Rivian started out by producing a high-end all-electric vehicle. The R1 truck was well received and won multiple awards. However, the volume was so low that the company lost money on every truck it sold. This is why the second step was to ramp up production, again, just like Tesla. That process went relatively well, leading to Rivian generating a gross profit.

A gross profit simply means that it made more money selling its trucks than it cost to make them. There are other costs to running a business, like selling, general, and administrative expenses and research and development costs. Achieving a gross profit was a huge step, but Rivian was still losing money as a business. That's where the R2 comes in.

To be a sustainably profitable company, Rivian needs to increase the number of cars it sells. That will allow it to spread its costs over more vehicles. However, the high-end of the market is limited, so Rivian needs a successful mass-market vehicle that costs less. That's what it was looking to create in the R2. It delivered, with the new vehicle helping to increase deliveries by 46% year over year in the third quarter of 2026. The R2 was Rivian's most popular model. This is a huge win.

What comes next for Rivian?

Rivian is clearly pleased with its results, but it is also realistic. High demand for the R2 is good, but it still needs to produce more vehicles. That means more capital spending is in the cards as the automaker continues to invest to expand its manufacturing capabilities. To that end, the company is building a new auto plant in Georgia. It probably won't be up and running until late 2028.

So, in the near term, the start-up is likely to continue to bleed red ink. Until it is sustainably profitable, stock gains will likely be limited. But each step closer to the end goal could see investors reward Rivian with a higher stock price. And, assuming the Georgia plant investment goes well, it isn't unreasonable to believe that Rivian could be sustainably profitable by the end of the decade or early in the 2030s.

Elon Musk lost about $113 billion of paper wealth in two days as Tesla and SpaceX fell after Democrats won the House and Senate.

A 63-year-old with $400,000 of his $1,000,000 in one stock on Tesla's path was down about $72,000 by Thursday's close; at 20% in the stock he would have lost $50,000.

The plan: hold through the drop, then trim about $171,000 in four pieces of about $43,000, taking regular withdrawals from the stock first.

Elon Musk lost about $113 billion of paper wealth in two days this week, $33.5 billion on Wednesday and $79.7 billion on Thursday, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index as reported by Fortune. Tesla and SpaceX together shed about $456 billion of market value between election night and Thursday's close after Democrats won the House and Senate.

Musk's fortune rides on two companies he runs. The household version of that problem is a 63-year-old retiree with $1,000,000 on election night: $400,000 in one stock he bought years ago that ran up, $600,000 in an S&P 500 index fund, and a plan to withdraw 4%, or $40,000 a year. If his stock had followed Tesla's path this week, he was down about $72,000 by Thursday's close, 7.2% of the $1,000,000 he started the week with, and 1.8 years of withdrawals gone in two sessions.

Shutterstock

The answer for him: hold through the drop day, then cut the stock to 20% of savings over the coming months, about $171,000 of sales in pieces, with the tax bill in view. Had he already been at 20%, Thursday's loss would have been $50,000 instead of $72,000.

What the two days cost a one-stock retiree

Closing prices show Tesla fell 3.34% Wednesday and 10.77% Thursday, 13.75% over the two days. The S&P 500 fund rose 1.65% Wednesday and fell 4.41% Thursday, 2.83% over the two days.

title: Elon Musk Wants to Build an "Enormous Robot Army." Here's What That Means for Tesla and SpaceX Investors.

Elon Musk Wants to Build an "Enormous Robot Army." Here's What That Means for Tesla and SpaceX Investors.
Ryan Vanzo, The Motley Fool

TSLA
SPCX
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Last year, Elon Musk stressed his priority of regaining majority voting control over Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA). His biggest concern at the time was control over new products -- humanoid robots, in particular -- that Tesla is expected to produce en masse over the coming years.

"My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ​ousted at some point in the future?" Musk told investors last October.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Whether investors agree with Musk's concern or not, it is clear that he seeks majority control over Tesla's daily operations. This has one major implication for shareholders of both Tesla and SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX).

A SpaceX and Tesla merger may not be in the interest of shareholders

While a merger between SpaceX and Tesla has not been formally announced, speculation of a potential tie-up has risen sharply after the companies launched independent committees focused on exploring the benefits of a merger.

Musk's negotiated pay package at Tesla originally included key milestones that would trigger additional stock grants, including the deployment of one million humanoid robots. But some experts are claiming that Musk's ambitious "enormous robot army" is a distraction from his true goal.

"It's irrelevant," Charles Elson, ​founding director of the Weinberg Center, told Reuters this week. "This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control."

Image source: Getty Images.

Musk's pay package with SpaceX grants him additional voting power before the shares are even issued. Incorporating the new pay package, Musk now has approximately 85% voting power at SpaceX. With roughly 20% voting power at Tesla, a tie-up between the two companies could ultimately give Musk majority control over the combined entity.

SpaceX's IPO prospectus was replete with bold long-term plans. Tesla, meanwhile, is working to sustain its lofty valuation with promises of robot armies and ubiquitous self-driving cars. Investors, however, should look deeper into these claims, understanding that a mega-merger between Tesla and SpaceX may have more to do with Musk's economic incentives than the best interests of shareholders.

Prediction: Tesla’s FSD Attach Rate Will “Trend to 100%.” But Will It Be Enough to Save the Stock?

Prediction: Tesla's FSD Attach Rate Will "Trend to 100%." But Will It Be Enough to Save the Stock? ©@Omar_Nasif from pixabay via Canva, @Diego Maravilla © 2022 from Diego Maravilla via Canva
Key Takeaways

Over 75% of Tesla's new North American deliveries in the third quarter came with FSD, up from over 55% in the second.

Venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson predicts that attach rate will "trend to 100%."

FSD is nearing $1 billion of annual recurring revenue, about 1% of Tesla's sales, so it helps margins more than growth.

At a forward P/E far above its five-year average, the stock needs Robotaxi, which Elon Musk expects to show up in results around the second quarter of 2027.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) fell 3.3% on Nov. 4 and another 10.8% on Nov. 5, closing at $343.69, after Democrats swept Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms and AI and chip stocks sold off.

Tesla's bulls would rather talk about a different number. Over 75% of Tesla's new North American deliveries in the third quarter came with FSD (Supervised), up from over 55% in the second quarter. Tesla said it believes FSD "is driving demand in markets where it is available."

Steve Jurvetson, an early Tesla investor and former Tesla director, went further on X:

"As we are on a path to the inevitable near future where FSD will be the sole purchase criteria, it follows that the attach rate for that sole purchase criteria will trend to 100%"

There's a catch. Every new Tesla comes with a free month of FSD, though the CFO said those buyers signed up for a paid subscription at delivery. An RBC analyst estimated the paid rate at 30% to 40%, and Tesla didn't address that number directly.

A Billion Dollars Doesn't Go Far at Tesla

On the third-quarter call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja agreed with New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu that FSD is nearing $1 billion of annual recurring revenue. Against $103.6 billion of revenue over the last 12 months, that's about 1% of the business, and analysts expect the business to get a lot bigger:

TSLA Revenue, Actual and Consensus Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's about $51 billion of growth from 2025 to 2028. Even if FSD's run rate doubled, it would add only about $1 billion a year.

Where FSD helps is margin, and Tesla needs the help, because its share of US EV sales has been slipping.

Gary Black of The Future Fund replied on X to a bull who said no one is near FSD that bulls "said the same thing about competitors catching TSLA on building out EVs, but that turned out to be false as Chinese EV manufacturers were able to quickly match TSLA on manufactured cost."
